title: BORG Drink: What It Is, How Strong It Is, and the Real Risks
excerpt: What a BORG (blackout rage gallon) actually is, how many drinks are in one, which harm-reduction claims hold up, why jungle juice hangovers hit so hard, and the alcohol poisoning signs to know.
metaDescription: What is a BORG drink? How many standard drinks are in one, which safety claims hold up, why jungle juice hangovers are so bad, and when to call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a BORG ("blackout rage gallon") is a plastic gallon jug of water with some of the water poured out and replaced with liquor, usually vodka, plus a flavored water enhancer and often an electrolyte powder. It got popular on TikTok and at college parties because it looks like a safer way to drink: it has a lid, it's your own jug, and it's mostly water. The problem is the amount of alcohol. The versions people usually describe contain roughly a full 750 mL bottle of vodka, which works out to around 17 standard drinks in one container. A lid and some electrolytes don't change what that much alcohol does to your body.

This guide is written for adults of legal drinking age. It won't give you a recipe. It explains what's actually in a BORG, which of the "harm reduction" claims hold up, why jungle juice hangovers feel so brutal, and the signs that mean someone needs medical help right now.

> **When to call for help.** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if someone who has been drinking **can't be woken up, is confused or unresponsive, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, is having a seizure, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute, or long gaps between breaths), or has cold, clammy, pale, or bluish skin.** These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which can kill. Don't leave the person alone to "sleep it off," and don't try cold showers or coffee. Turn them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them until help arrives. You can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) for advice. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## What Is a BORG Drink?

BORG stands for **blackout rage gallon**. The name is a joke, but it's also a fair description of what can happen if you drink the whole thing.

The basic idea, as it's described online, is simple. You start with a sealed one-gallon jug of water, pour some of the water out, add liquor, and then add a flavored liquid water enhancer to cover the taste. Many people also add an electrolyte powder, the kind sold as hydration mixes. Then you write your name or a pun on the jug with a marker, which became part of the trend. Every person carries their own jug around the party.

BORGs spread quickly in 2023, mostly through short videos from college students. Part of the appeal was that they were pitched as a *responsible* alternative to the party punch bowl. That pitch is where most of the confusion comes from, so it's worth looking at each claim on its own.

## How Much Alcohol Is in a BORG?

This is the most important part of the page, and it's the part the trend videos tend to skip.

A standard drink in the US contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

- 12 oz of regular beer (about 5% alcohol)
- 5 oz of wine (about 12% alcohol)
- 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor (40% alcohol), a single shot

A 750 mL bottle of 80-proof vodka holds about 300 mL of pure alcohol. Divide that by the amount in one standard drink and you get **about 17 standard drinks**. The versions of the BORG that circulate most widely use around that much liquor. Some people use half a bottle, which is still about 8 or 9 standard drinks. Some use more.

To put that in context, US health guidance from the Dietary Guidelines for Americans and the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) describes binge drinking as about 4 or more drinks for women or 5 or more for men in roughly two hours. A full-strength BORG is three to four times that amount in one jug.

| What's in the jug | Rough standard drinks |
|---|---|
| A full 750 mL bottle of 80-proof vodka | About 17 |
| Half a 750 mL bottle | About 8 to 9 |
| A 375 mL bottle (a "pint") | About 8 to 9 |
| Four shots (6 oz) of 80-proof liquor | About 4 |

The extra water doesn't reduce the number of drinks. Diluting alcohol makes each sip weaker, but if you finish the jug, you've still taken in every gram of alcohol that went into it. Water only changes how fast you get there.

## The Harm-Reduction Claims, Checked

BORGs got a reputation as a "safer" way to party. Some of that is real. Some of it isn't. Here's an honest look at each claim.

### "It has a lid, so nobody can spike it." Partly true.

A sealed jug that you keep in your hand is harder to tamper with than an open cup or a shared punch bowl. That's a genuine advantage, especially compared with jungle juice, where anyone can add anything to the bowl. But the protection only lasts as long as the jug stays with you. Put it down on a counter for twenty minutes and it's no safer than any other drink. Drink spiking is also less common than over-drinking as a cause of people ending up in the hospital after parties. The most common danger in the jug is the alcohol you put there yourself.

### "You know exactly what's in it." True, if you made it.

With jungle juice, you have no idea how much liquor went into the bowl or what kind. With your own BORG, you do. That's useful information. It only helps, though, if you use it. Knowing your jug contains 17 drinks doesn't help you if you still plan to finish it.

### "It's mostly water, so you stay hydrated." Misleading.

It's true that a gallon jug holds a lot of water. But you can't separate the water from the alcohol once they're mixed. Every sip that hydrates you also contains liquor. If you drink the jug at a pace that would hydrate you well, you also drink a dangerous amount of alcohol. If you drink it slowly enough to stay safe, you aren't getting much water. Plain water on the side, in a separate bottle, is a much better tool for staying hydrated.

### "The electrolytes stop the hangover." Not really.

Alcohol makes you urinate more because it suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. So some fluid and salt loss is part of a heavy night. Electrolyte mixes can help replace that. But dehydration is only one piece of a hangover. Research reviews on hangovers point to several other factors, including the body's inflammatory response, broken sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, and acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol. There is no good evidence that adding electrolytes to a drink prevents a hangover. Our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when they actually help.

### "Everyone has their own jug, so nobody shares germs." Usually not how it goes.

In theory, a personal jug means no shared cups. In practice, people pass jugs around at parties. If you're sharing a BORG, you're sharing saliva too, and you also lose track of how much you drank.

## Why BORGs Can Still Go Badly Wrong

Even a person who means well can get into trouble with a BORG. The format itself pushes in the wrong direction in a few ways.

### The flavor hides the alcohol

Water enhancers are strongly flavored. That's the point: they make the drink taste like fruit punch instead of vodka. When you can't taste the alcohol, you lose one of the natural signals that would slow you down. People often describe BORGs as "going down easy," which is exactly the problem.

### The container has no natural stopping point

A can of beer ends. A glass of wine ends. A gallon jug is so big that most people never get near the bottom, which makes it hard to notice how much you've had. Drinking from a container with no clear end tends to make people lose count.

### Some enhancers and add-ins contain caffeine

Some flavored water enhancers come in caffeinated "energy" versions, and some people add energy drinks. Caffeine doesn't sober you up. It can make you feel more alert than you really are, which researchers sometimes describe as being "wide-awake drunk." The CDC warns that mixing alcohol with energy drinks is linked to drinking more and to riskier behavior, because people don't feel as intoxicated as they actually are. Their reaction time and judgment are still impaired. If you're checking labels, skip anything with caffeine.

### Your blood alcohol keeps climbing after you stop

Alcohol takes time to get from your stomach into your bloodstream. If you drink a lot quickly, your blood alcohol level can keep rising for a while after your last sip. Someone who seems fine at 11 p.m. can be in real danger by midnight. This is why "they were okay a minute ago" is not a reason to leave a very drunk person alone.

### Day-drinking on an empty stomach

BORGs are often a daytime party drink, and people often start before eating much. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Drinking on an empty stomach lets your blood alcohol rise faster and higher. If you're heading to a party, see our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).

### The real-world record

In March 2023, local officials in Amherst, Massachusetts reported dozens of ambulance calls to large off-campus parties near the University of Massachusetts, and BORGs were widely reported as a common drink at those gatherings. That incident is a big part of why the trend made national news. The lesson isn't that BORGs are uniquely evil. It's that a drink that hides a very large dose of alcohol behind a "healthy" image, at a party full of people drinking the same thing, is a recipe for a lot of people getting very drunk at once.

## Jungle Juice: What It Is and Why the Hangover Is So Bad

Jungle juice is the older party drink that BORGs were partly meant to replace. It's usually a big shared container (a punch bowl, a cooler, sometimes a clean trash can) filled with several kinds of liquor, fruit juice, soda, and cut-up fruit. There is no fixed recipe, and that's exactly the issue.

People often say jungle juice gives them the worst hangover of their life. There are a few real reasons why.

### You have no idea how strong it is

Whoever made the jungle juice might have used two bottles or six. Each cup could hold one drink's worth of alcohol or three. When you can't measure, you can't pace yourself. Most bad jungle juice hangovers are really just the result of drinking much more alcohol than you thought.

### The sugar hides the alcohol

Fruit juice and soda make strong punch taste mild. Like the water enhancers in a BORG, sweetness makes it easy to drink fast. There's no good evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers, but sweet mixers make it much easier to overdo the alcohol.

One related finding: a small study by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that people who drank vodka mixed with a diet soda reached a higher breath alcohol level than when they drank the same amount of vodka mixed with a regular sugary soda. Sugar in the stomach seems to slow how fast alcohol is absorbed a little. So "diet" mixers aren't a safer choice, and some BORG water enhancers are sugar-free.

### Mixing liquors isn't the main problem

Many people blame the combination of different spirits. The evidence doesn't really back that up. A randomized study published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* in 2019 tested the old "beer before liquor" rule and found that the order of drinks made no real difference to how bad the hangover was. What mattered most was how much people drank and how drunk they got. You can read more in our article on the [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

### Darker liquors may add a little

Alcoholic drinks contain small amounts of other compounds made during fermentation and aging, called congeners. Darker spirits like bourbon and brandy tend to have more of them than clear spirits like vodka. A study by Damaris Rohsenow and colleagues, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010, found that people rated their hangovers somewhat worse after bourbon than after the same amount of vodka. If jungle juice includes dark rum or whiskey, that may play a small role. But the effect in that study was modest compared with the effect of the total amount of alcohol. A gallon of vodka still causes a terrible hangover. For more on this, see our guide on [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

### The open bowl is a spiking risk

Anyone at the party can add something to a shared bowl, including more alcohol or drugs. You can't check what's in it. This is the one area where a sealed, personal container really is safer.

## BORG vs. Jungle Juice

| | BORG | Jungle juice |
|---|---|---|
| Who controls the alcohol | You, if you made it | Whoever made the bowl |
| Can you count your drinks? | Yes, in theory | Not really |
| Spiking risk | Lower while the jug stays in your hand | Higher in an open shared bowl |
| Typical strength | Often around 17 standard drinks per jug | Unknown, varies batch to batch |
| What hides the alcohol | Flavored water enhancers | Juice, soda, fruit |
| Hangover drivers | Total amount of alcohol, broken sleep, caffeine if added | Total amount of alcohol, unknown strength, possibly darker spirits |

Neither drink is "safe" in the amounts people usually drink them. The BORG's real advantage is that you can control what goes in. That only helps if you choose to put in less.

## If You're Going to Drink One: A Lower-Risk Approach

If you're of legal drinking age and you're going to a party where BORGs are the thing, here's how to keep the idea and drop most of the risk. None of this makes heavy drinking safe, but it can make a big difference.

1. **Put in far less alcohol.** The single biggest change you can make. The jug doesn't need to hold a whole bottle. Measure what you add, and know how many standard drinks it equals before you leave the house. Using the table above, a few shots' worth is a very different night from a full bottle.
2. **Decide your limit before you start, and write it on the jug.** You're already writing on it. Draw a line at the level where you'll stop.
3. **Skip anything with caffeine.** Check the label on the water enhancer and leave out energy drinks.
4. **Eat a real meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
5. **Carry a separate bottle of plain water.** That's what actually keeps you hydrated, without adding alcohol.
6. **Keep the jug with you, and don't share it.** If you set it down and lose track of it, start fresh with a sealed bottle of water.
7. **Pace yourself over hours, not minutes.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, and that's not something you can speed up.
8. **Have a plan for getting home.** Never drive after drinking. Agree on a ride before the party starts.
9. **Look out for your friends.** If someone is getting very drunk, help them stop, and know the warning signs below.

## Signs of Alcohol Poisoning: Know Them Before the Party

Alcohol poisoning happens when there's so much alcohol in the blood that the parts of the brain that control basic functions, like breathing, heart rate, and temperature, start to shut down. It's a medical emergency. NIAAA and other health agencies list these warning signs:

- Confusion or stupor (very slow to respond)
- Trouble staying awake, or can't be woken up
- Vomiting, especially while drowsy or passed out
- Seizures
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregular breathing (10 seconds or more between breaths)
- Slow heart rate
- Clammy, pale, or bluish skin, especially on the lips or fingertips
- Low body temperature
- Loss of bladder control

**A person doesn't need to have every sign.** If someone has even a few of them, or you're unsure, call 911. It's far better to make a call that turns out not to be needed than to wait.

While you wait for help:

- **Stay with them.** Don't leave them alone to sleep it off.
- **Turn them on their side** (the recovery position) so they won't choke if they vomit.
- **Don't give them more alcohol, coffee, or a cold shower.** None of these help, and some can make things worse.
- **Tell responders what and how much they drank** if you know, including whether there were drugs or medicines involved.

Many states and colleges have "medical amnesty" or Good Samaritan policies that offer some protection to people who call for help during an alcohol emergency. The details vary by place, so check your state's or school's policy. Fear of getting in trouble should never be the reason someone doesn't get help.

## The Next Morning: Recovering From a BORG or Jungle Juice Night

If you drank too much and wake up with a hangover, the basics are the same as any other hangover. There's no fast cure, but you can make yourself more comfortable.

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water, an oral rehydration drink, or broth. Small sips if you feel sick.
- **Eat something easy.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, or soup. Your blood sugar can run low after heavy drinking.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen can irritate a stomach that's already upset, and acetaminophen (Tylenol) is harder on the liver after heavy drinking. Stick to the label dose, take it with food, and don't stack products.
- **Rest.** Alcohol breaks up deep sleep, so much of the tiredness is real sleep loss.
- **Don't drive.** After a very heavy night, you may still be over the legal limit the next morning, even if you feel okay.

**See a doctor if** you keep vomiting and can't keep water down, you see blood in your vomit, you have severe stomach pain, you feel confused, or you feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious with a racing heart that doesn't settle. Those aren't normal hangover symptoms and they're worth checking out.

For a fuller plan for future nights out, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Where DHM Fits (Honestly)

Some people who go to big parties take a DHM (dihydromyricetin) supplement. DHM is a plant compound found in Japanese raisin tree extract. Lab and animal studies suggest it may affect how the body processes alcohol and how alcohol acts on the brain, and there's a small amount of human research. It's an interesting area, but the human evidence is limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people drinking the amounts in a full BORG.

It's also worth being completely clear about what DHM doesn't do. It **does not** lower your blood alcohol, it does not make you less impaired, it won't make it safe to drive, and it offers no protection against alcohol poisoning. The only thing that does that is drinking less.

If you want to try DHM as one part of a sensible plan for a moderate night, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you're a student on a tight budget, our [college student DHM guide](/never-hungover/college-student-dhm-guide-2025) is a good place to start.

## The Bottom Line

- A BORG is a gallon jug of water mixed with liquor and flavoring. The widely shared versions hold around **17 standard drinks**.
- The lid and personal jug do lower the risk of spiking, and you know what's inside. Those are real benefits.
- The water and electrolytes don't cancel out the alcohol. There is no good evidence they prevent a hangover.
- Flavoring, caffeine, and a container with no natural end make it easy to drink far more than you meant to.
- Jungle juice hangovers are bad mainly because nobody knows how strong the punch is. Mixing liquors matters much less than the total amount.
- If you drink a BORG, put in much less alcohol, skip caffeine, eat first, carry plain water, and keep the jug with you.
- Know the signs of alcohol poisoning. If someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly, is vomiting while drowsy, or has a seizure, call 911 and stay with them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What does BORG stand for?**

BORG stands for "blackout rage gallon." It's a plastic gallon jug of water with some of the water replaced by liquor, usually vodka, plus a flavored water enhancer and often an electrolyte powder. People carry their own labeled jug at parties. The trend spread on TikTok and at college parties in 2023.

**How many drinks are in a BORG?**

It depends on how much liquor goes in, but the widely shared versions use about a 750 mL bottle of 80-proof vodka. That's roughly 17 US standard drinks in one jug. Half a bottle is still about 8 or 9 standard drinks. Adding water makes each sip weaker, but finishing the jug means drinking all of the alcohol that went into it.

**Is a BORG safer than other party drinks?**

In a couple of ways, yes. A sealed jug you keep in your hand is harder to spike than an open punch bowl, and if you made it, you know what's in it. But the usual BORG holds a very large amount of alcohol, and the flavoring makes it easy to drink fast. A BORG is only lower-risk if you put much less alcohol in it, skip caffeine, and pace yourself.

**Do the electrolytes in a BORG prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that adding electrolytes to an alcoholic drink prevents a hangover. Electrolytes can help replace fluid and salt lost because alcohol makes you urinate more, but hangovers also come from inflammation, poor sleep, stomach irritation, and acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol. Drinking plain water from a separate bottle is a better way to stay hydrated.

**Why does jungle juice give such bad hangovers?**

Mostly because nobody knows how strong it is. Jungle juice mixes several liquors with juice and soda in a shared container, so each cup can hold far more alcohol than you'd guess, and the sweetness hides it. Research on mixing drinks suggests the order or combination of drinks matters much less than the total amount of alcohol. Darker liquors may add a little to hangover severity, but the main cause is simply drinking a lot.

**Can a BORG cause alcohol poisoning?**

Yes. A full-strength BORG holds enough alcohol to cause alcohol poisoning, especially if it's drunk quickly or on an empty stomach. Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is confused, is vomiting while drowsy, has a seizure, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or has pale or bluish skin. Turn them on their side and stay with them until help arrives.

**Is it bad to put caffeine or energy drinks in a BORG?**

Yes, it's best to skip them. Caffeine doesn't sober you up. It can make you feel more alert than you are, so you may keep drinking and take more risks while your judgment and reaction time are still impaired. The CDC warns that mixing alcohol with energy drinks is linked to drinking more. Some water enhancers come in caffeinated versions, so check the label.

**Does DHM help if you drink a BORG?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers at the amounts in a full BORG. DHM does not lower blood alcohol, does not reduce impairment, and offers no protection against alcohol poisoning. Some people use it as one part of a plan for a moderate night, but the most effective step is putting much less alcohol in the jug.
